content: The minor histocompatibility antigen H13 is a protein in humans encoded by the HM13 gene. This antigen is a nonamer peptide derived from a protein encoded by the H13 gene. The peptide is produced in the cytosol by the proteasome, transported into the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) via the transporter associated with antigen processing (TAP), and subsequently presented on the cell surface by H2-Db major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC I) molecules. In mice, the alloreactivity that leads to transplant rejection is mediated by a Val/Ile polymorphism in the peptide sequence ‘SSV(V/I)GVWYL.’ The human ortholog of this gene is called HM13. However, it remains unclear whether a similar polymorphism exists in humans and whether HM13 functions as a minor histocompatibility antigen in humans. The protein encoded by the M13/HM13 gene is the signal peptide peptidase (SPP), an intramembrane protease that resides in the ER. SPP is localized to the endoplasmic reticulum and catalyzes the intramembrane proteolysis of certain signal peptides after they have been cleaved from a preprotein. This enzymatic activity is essential for generating signal sequence-derived human lymphocyte antigen-E (HLA-E) epitopes, which are recognized by the immune system, and for processing the core protein of the hepatitis C virus. The encoded protein is an integral membrane protein with sequence motifs characteristic of presenilin-type aspartic proteases. Additionally, multiple transcript variants encoding several distinct isoforms of this protein have been identified.
